newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinian lawmakers pass Arafat's budget.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian lawmakers pass Arafat's budget.

text.p: Palestinian lawmakers passed the Palestinian Authority's 1997 budget on Tuesday after hours of stormy debate over amounts allocated to President Yasser Arafat and his police.
The Palestinian Legislative Council approved the $866 million budget Finance Minister Mohammad al-Nashashibi had proposed after taking off $8 million from the $248 draft police budget.
Eleven percent of the total budget figure, which includes a $52 million deficit, was allotted to Arafat's office, which includes 21 departments.

"Why should the budget of the president's office be given special privileges. This (the deficit) is a violation of the bylaws of the council and I am sorry we are dealing with it this way," said lawmaker Hatem Abdel-Qader.
The Council's financial committee had suggested lowering Arafat's budget from 11 to 8.5 percent of the budget, but Speaker of the Council Ahmed Korei rejected the proposal.
"Frankly, we should not touch the budget of the president," he said.
Legislator Azmi Shoaibi announced he was resigning from the financial committee in protest, but the council adopted Korei's proposal.
"Why are you worried about the deficit. The president will himself find a way to get the extra money," said legislator Marwan Barghouthi, causing laughter in the council.
It was the first time Arafat's budget had ever been discussed or approved.
Lawmakers in the 88-member council, elected last year, have accused some ministers in Arafat's administration of corruption.
The Palestinian leader's policies have generally gone unchallenged in his more than 30 years of rule over the PLO.
Most of the $240 million allocated to the PLO's multiple police and security branches would be spent on salaries and headquarters, legislators said.

The 1993 PLO-Israel peace deals stipulated the Palestinian police force, composed primarily of former PLO guerrilla fighters who arrived from exile, would reach no more than 35,000 men in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, but in Gaza alone there are at least 30,000 troops.

"The Palestinian Authority increased the number of policemen not because they are trained and qualified but because all the fighters who returned had no jobs and because many youths were unemployed, so joining the police was one way of giving them a salary to feed their families," a PLO official said.
